claim: Mineral malnutrition stemming from undiversified plant-based diets is a top global challenge.
source: Mineral malnutrition stemming from undiversified plant-based diets is a top global challenge.
evidence: This is a statement about the global significance of mineral malnutrition, drawing on established understanding in nutrition and public health.

claim: In C3 plants (e.g., rice, wheat), elevated concentrations of atmospheric carbon dioxide (eCO2) reduce protein and nitrogen concentrations.
source: In C3 plants (e.g., rice, wheat), elevated concentrations of atmospheric carbon dioxide (eCO2) reduce protein and nitrogen concentrations, and can increase the total non-structural carbohydrates (TNC; mainly starch, sugars).
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analysis data presented in the manuscript showing nitrogen reductions in C3 plants under eCO2.

claim: Elevated CO2 can increase the total non-structural carbohydrates (TNC; mainly starch, sugars) in C3 plants.
source: In C3 plants (e.g., rice, wheat), elevated concentrations of atmospheric carbon dioxide (eCO2) reduce protein and nitrogen concentrations, and can increase the total non-structural carbohydrates (TNC; mainly starch, sugars).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to previous studies and data discussed in the manuscript regarding TNC increases.

claim: eCO2 reduces the overall mineral concentrations by −8% (95% confidence interval: −9.1 to −6.9, p<0.00001) in C3 plants.
source: This study shows that eCO2 reduces the overall mineral concentrations (−8%, 95% confidence interval: −9.1 to −6.9, p<0.00001) and increases TNC:minerals > carbon:minerals in C3 plants.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the meta-analysis of 7761 observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: eCO2 increases TNC:minerals ratio in C3 plants.
source: This study shows that eCO2 reduces the overall mineral concentrations (−8%, 95% confidence interval: −9.1 to −6.9, p<0.00001) and increases TNC:minerals > carbon:minerals in C3 plants.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing mineral reductions and TNC increases under eCO2.

claim: The meta-analysis covers 7761 observations, including 2264 observations at state of the art FACE centers.
source: The meta-analysis of 7761 observations, including 2264 observations at state of the art FACE centers, covers 130 species/cultivars.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset size used in the study.

claim: The meta-analysis covers 130 species/cultivars.
source: The meta-analysis of 7761 observations, including 2264 observations at state of the art FACE centers, covers 130 species/cultivars.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the taxonomic breadth of the dataset.

claim: C3 plants account for over three quarters of global primary production.
source: The bulk of the terrestrial conversion of CO2-to-carbohydrates is done by C3 plants, which account for over three quarters of global primary production and for over 90% of Earth's plant species (Still and Berry, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Still and Berry, 2003.

claim: C3 plants account for over 90% of Earth's plant species.
source: The bulk of the terrestrial conversion of CO2-to-carbohydrates is done by C3 plants, which account for over three quarters of global primary production and for over 90% of Earth's plant species (Still and Berry, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Still and Berry, 2003.

claim: When exposed to CO2 concentrations twice the preindustrial level of ∼280 ppm, plants increase the synthesis of carbohydrates by 19–46%.
source: When exposed to CO2 concentrations twice the preindustrial level of ∼280 ppm, plants increase the synthesis of carbohydrates by 19–46% (Leakey et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leakey et al., 2009.

claim: Currently, CO2 concentrations are reaching 400 ppm—the highest level since the dawn of agriculture and likely to be the highest since the rise of modern humans.
source: Currently, CO2 concentrations are reaching 400 ppm—the highest level since the dawn of agriculture and likely to be the highest since the rise of modern humans (Siegenthaler et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Siegenthaler et al., 2005.

claim: Within a single human lifespan, CO2 levels are projected to reach 421–936 ppm.
source: Within a single human lifespan, CO2 levels are projected to reach 421–936 ppm (IPCC, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to IPCC, 2013.

claim: Elevated CO2 effects on plant quantity (productivity and total biomass) have been extensively studied and show higher agricultural yields for crops, including wheat, rice, barley, and potato.
source: Elevated CO2 effects on plant quantity (productivity and total biomass) have been extensively studied and show higher agricultural yields for crops, including wheat, rice, barley, and potato.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the existing body of research on eCO2 effects on crop yields.

claim: IPCC (2007, 2013) and AAAC Climate Science Panel (2014) include direct CO2 effects (e.g., ocean acidification) in their climate change assessments but do not mention any CO2 effects on crop or wild plant quality.
source: Notably, IPCC (2007, 2013) and AAAC Climate Science Panel (2014) include direct CO2 effects (e.g., ocean acidification) in their climate change assessments but do not mention any CO2 effects on crop or wild plant quality.
evidence: This claim is based on citations to IPCC reports and AAAC Climate Science Panel.

claim: The stoichiometry—the relative ratios of chemical elements—in plants is plastic and, to a considerable degree, reflects their environment.
source: The stoichiometry—the relative ratios of chemical elements—in plants is plastic and, to a considerable degree, reflects their environment (Sterner and Elser, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sterner and Elser, 2002.

claim: The inter-laboratory variance for nitrogen analysis was 6.5%, but twice as large for phosphorus and calcium, and reached 130% for sodium.
source: For example, Stefan et al. (1997) report the accuracy test for 39 facilities that analyzed samples of the same plant tissues: the inter-laboratory variance was 6.5% for N, but twice as large for phosphorus (P) and calcium (Ca), and reached 130% for sodium (Na).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stefan et al., 1997.

claim: The first empirical evidence of lower mineral content in plants exposed to eCO2 appeared at least over a quarter century ago.
source: The first empirical evidence of lower mineral content in plants exposed to eCO2 appeared at least over a quarter century ago (e.g., Porter and Grodzinski, 1984; Peet et al., 1986; O'Neill et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Porter and Grodzinski, 1984; Peet et al., 1986; O'Neill et al., 1987.

claim: Physiological mechanisms responsible for the overall decline of plant mineral content include increased carbohydrate production combined with other eCO2 effects such as reduced transpiration.
source: Physiological mechanisms responsible for the overall decline of plant mineral content—with expected changes being non-uniform across minerals—have been proposed: the increased carbohydrate production combined with other eCO2 effects such as reduced transpiration (Loladze, 2002; McGrath and Lobell, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Loladze, 2002; McGrath and Lobell, 2013.

claim: Lieffering et al. (2004) found no decline in any of the minerals but lower N content in the grains of rice harvested at four FACE paddies in Japan.
source: In the grains of rice harvested at four FACE paddies in Japan, Lieffering et al. (2004) found no decline in any of the minerals but lower N content.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lieffering et al., 2004.

claim: Seneweera and Conroy (1997) were the first to report lower iron (Fe) and zinc (Zn) in grains of rice grown at eCO2.
source: The result disagreed with Seneweera and Conroy (1997), who were the first to report lower iron (Fe) and zinc (Zn) in grains of rice grown at eCO2 and warned that altered rice quality can negatively affect developing countries.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Seneweera and Conroy, 1997.

claim: Elevated CO2 reduces N concentrations by 10–18% systemically throughout various tissues: leaves, stems, roots, tubers, reproductive and edible parts, including seeds and grains.
source: Elevated CO2 reduces N concentrations by 10–18% systemically throughout various tissues: leaves, stems, roots, tubers, reproductive and edible parts, including seeds and grains (Cotrufo et al., 1998; Jablonski et al., 2002; Taub et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cotrufo et al., 1998; Jablonski et al., 2002; Taub et al., 2008.

claim: eCO2 can further lower N concentrations in plants by reducing concentrations of Rubisco—one of the most abundant proteins on Earth that comprises a sizable N-pool in plants.
source: In addition to the carbohydrate dilution and reduced transpiration, eCO2 can further lower N concentrations in plants by: (1) reducing concentrations of Rubisco—one of the most abundant proteins on Earth that comprises a sizable N-pool in plants (Drake et al., 1997), and (2) inhibiting nitrate assimilation (Bloom et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Drake et al., 1997.

claim: eCO2 can lower N concentrations in plants by inhibiting nitrate assimilation.
source: In addition to the carbohydrate dilution and reduced transpiration, eCO2 can further lower N concentrations in plants by: (1) reducing concentrations of Rubisco—one of the most abundant proteins on Earth that comprises a sizable N-pool in plants (Drake et al., 1997), and (2) inhibiting nitrate assimilation (Bloom et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bloom et al., 2010.

claim: In the largest to date meta-analysis on the issue by Duval et al. (2011), who fragmented data from 56 eCO2 studies into 67 cases, in 47 of the cases, the effect of eCO2 on minerals was statistically non-significant.
source: The obscure nature of the effect of eCO2 on minerals becomes particularly apparent in the largest to date meta-analysis on the issue by Duval et al. (2011), who fragmented data from 56 eCO2 studies into 67 cases. In 47 of the cases, the effect of eCO2 on minerals was statistically non-significant, that is the 95% Confidence Interval (CI) for the effect size overlapped with 0.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Duval et al., 2011.

claim: Duval et al. (2011) concluded: 'A major finding of this synthesis is the lack of effect of CO2 on crop grains nutrient concentration'.
source: Duval et al. (2011) concluded: "A major finding of this synthesis is the lack of effect of CO2 on crop grains nutrient concentration".
evidence: This is a direct quote from Duval et al., 2011.

claim: Every statistically significant increase in mineral concentrations in Duval et al. (2011) was obtained by bootstrapping a sample of size 2, 4 or 5.
source: However, a closer examination of the results of Duval et al. (2011) reveals that every statistically significant increase in mineral concentrations was obtained by bootstrapping a sample of size 2, 4 or 5—a recipe for generating invalid 95% CIs.
evidence: This is an observation made by the author based on examination of Duval et al., 2011.

claim: False research findings, stemming from small sample sizes and associated low statistical power, are a persistent problem in biomedical sciences.
source: Ioannidis (2005) showed that false research findings, stemming from small sample sizes and associated low statistical power, are a persistent problem in biomedical sciences.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ioannidis, 2005.

claim: The probability of a research finding to reflect a true effect drops drastically if the statistical power is reduced from 0.80 to low levels, for example <0.30.
source: Calling the problem as 'power failure', Button et al. (2013) emphasized that the probability of a research finding to reflect a true effect drops drastically if the statistical power is reduced from 0.80 (considered as appropriate) to low levels, for example <0.30.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Button et al., 2013.

claim: Across all the data, eCO2 reduced concentrations of P, potassium (K), Ca, S, magnesium (Mg), Fe, Zn, and copper (Cu) by 6.5–10% (p<0.0001).
source: Across all the data, eCO2 reduced concentrations of P, potassium (K), Ca, S, magnesium (Mg), Fe, Zn, and copper (Cu) by 6.5–10% (p<0.0001) as shown on Figure 2.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the meta-analysis presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Only manganese (Mn) showed no significant change under eCO2.
source: Only manganese (Mn) showed no significant change.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Among all the measured elements, only C increased (6%, 2.6 to 10.4, p<0.01) under eCO2.
source: Among all the measured elements, only C increased (6%, 2.6 to 10.4, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Among all elements, N declined the most (−15%, −17.8 to −13.1, p<0.00001) under eCO2.
source: As expected, among all elements N declined the most (−15%, −17.8 to −13.1, p<0.00001) (Figure 2), matching very closely previous findings (Figures 3–6): the 17–19% decline in leaves found by Cotrufo et al. (1998) and the 14% decline in seeds found by Jablonski et al. (2002).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The 15% decline in N found in this study matches very closely the 17–19% decline in leaves found by Cotrufo et al. (1998).
source: As expected, among all elements N declined the most (−15%, −17.8 to −13.1, p<0.00001) (Figure 2), matching very closely previous findings (Figures 3–6): the 17–19% decline in leaves found by Cotrufo et al. (1998) and the 14% decline in seeds found by Jablonski et al. (2002).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's findings with previous research cited.

claim: The 15% decline in N found in this study matches the 14% decline in seeds found by Jablonski et al. (2002).
source: As expected, among all elements N declined the most (−15%, −17.8 to −13.1, p<0.00001) (Figure 2), matching very closely previous findings (Figures 3–6): the 17–19% decline in leaves found by Cotrufo et al. (1998) and the 14% decline in seeds found by Jablonski et al. (2002).
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's findings with previous research cited.

claim: The lower N in edible tissues corroborates the protein declines in crops found by Taub et al. (2008).
source: Since the contents of N and protein correlate strongly in plant tissues, the lower N in edible tissues (Figure 4) corroborates the protein declines in crops found by Taub et al. (2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between N and protein, supported by citation to Taub et al., 2008.

claim: In both the FACE and the non-FACE studies eCO2 significantly reduced N, P, K, Ca, S, Mg, and Zn.
source: With respect to the types of experiments, the CO2 effect on the plant ionome is surprisingly robust: in both the FACE and the non-FACE studies eCO2 significantly reduced N, P, K, Ca, S, Mg, and Zn (Figures 5, 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis comparing FACE and non-FACE studies.

claim: The average level of eCO2 in the FACE studies was 560 ppm compared to 732 ppm in the non-FACE studies.
source: The high cost of CO2 required for running free-air experiments led to a much lower average level of eCO2 in the FACE studies (560 ppm) cf. 732 ppm in the non-FACE studies.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the CO2 levels used in different study types.

claim: The overall mineral decline in FACE studies was −6.1% (−7.8 to −4.4) compared to −8.7% (−10.1 to −7.4) for the non-FACE studies.
source: It is plausible that the lower levels of CO2 in the FACE studies contributed to a smaller overall mineral decline (−6.1%, −7.8 to −4.4) cf. (−8.7%, −10.1 to −7.4) for the non-FACE studies.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis comparing FACE and non-FACE studies.

claim: The mineral decline in the tropics and subtropics (−7.2%, −10.4 to −4.0, p<0.0001) is comparable to the decline in the temperate region (−6.4%, −7.9 to −5.0, p<0.00001).
source: The mineral decline in the tropics and subtropics (−7.2%, −10.4 to −4.0, p<0.0001) is comparable to the decline in the temperate region (−6.4%, −7.9 to −5.0, p<0.00001).
evidence: This is a finding from the geographical analysis of the meta-analysis data.

claim: With the exception of three small centers (in Bangladesh, Japan, and the UK), the mean mineral concentrations declined in every FACE and open top chamber (OTC) center on four continents.
source: With the exception of three small centers (in Bangladesh, Japan, and the UK), the mean mineral concentrations declined in every FACE and open top chamber (OTC) center on four continents.
evidence: This is a finding from the geographical analysis of the meta-analysis data.

claim: No statistically significant effect of eCO2 was found on the ionome of C4 plants.
source: Since eCO2 does not stimulate carbohydrate production in C4 plants to a degree that it does in C3 plants, one would expect a milder CO2 effect on minerals for C4 plants. Indeed, no statistically significant effect was found on the ionome of C4 plants (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis comparing C3 and C4 plants.

claim: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in crops (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6).
source: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in crops (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6); wild (−9.7%, −11.6 to −7.8), herbaceous (−7.5%, −8.7 to −5.6), and woody (−9.6%, −12.1 to −7.6) plants; foliar (−9.2%, −10.8 to −7.6) and edible (−6.4%, −7.8 to −5.1) tissues, including grains (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis for different plant groups.

claim: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in wild plants (−9.7%, −11.6 to −7.8).
source: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in crops (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6); wild (−9.7%, −11.6 to −7.8), herbaceous (−7.5%, −8.7 to −5.6), and woody (−9.6%, −12.1 to −7.6) plants; foliar (−9.2%, −10.8 to −7.6) and edible (−6.4%, −7.8 to −5.1) tissues, including grains (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis for different plant groups.

claim: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in herbaceous plants (−7.5%, −8.7 to −5.6).
source: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in crops (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6); wild (−9.7%, −11.6 to −7.8), herbaceous (−7.5%, −8.7 to −5.6), and woody (−9.6%, −12.1 to −7.6) plants; foliar (−9.2%, −10.8 to −7.6) and edible (−6.4%, −7.8 to −5.1) tissues, including grains (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis for different plant groups.

claim: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in woody plants (−9.6%, −12.1 to −7.6).
source: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in crops (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6); wild (−9.7%, −11.6 to −7.8), herbaceous (−7.5%, −8.7 to −5.6), and woody (−9.6%, −12.1 to −7.6) plants; foliar (−9.2%, −10.8 to −7.6) and edible (−6.4%, −7.8 to −5.1) tissues, including grains (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis for different plant groups.

claim: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in foliar tissues (−9.2%, −10.8 to −7.6).
source: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in crops (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6); wild (−9.7%, −11.6 to −7.8), herbaceous (−7.5%, −8.7 to −5.6), and woody (−9.6%, −12.1 to −7.6) plants; foliar (−9.2%, −10.8 to −7.6) and edible (−6.4%, −7.8 to −5.1) tissues, including grains (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis for different tissue types.

claim: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in edible tissues (−6.4%, −7.8 to −5.1).
source: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in crops (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6); wild (−9.7%, −11.6 to −7.8), herbaceous (−7.5%, −8.7 to −5.6), and woody (−9.6%, −12.1 to −7.6) plants; foliar (−9.2%, −10.8 to −7.6) and edible (−6.4%, −7.8 to −5.1) tissues, including grains (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis for different tissue types.

claim: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in grains (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6).
source: Elevated CO2 reduced the overall mineral concentrations in crops (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6); wild (−9.7%, −11.6 to −7.8), herbaceous (−7.5%, −8.7 to −5.6), and woody (−9.6%, −12.1 to −7.6) plants; foliar (−9.2%, −10.8 to −7.6) and edible (−6.4%, −7.8 to −5.1) tissues, including grains (−7.2%, −8.6 to −5.6).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis for grain tissues.

claim: The cereal specific decline in wheat grains is −7.6% (−9.3 to −5.9).
source: The cereal specific declines in grains are as follows: wheat (−7.6%, −9.3 to −5.9), rice (−7.2%, −11.3 to −3.1), and barley (−6.9%, −10.5 to −3.2) (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis for specific cereal crops.

claim: The cereal specific decline in rice grains is −7.2% (−11.3 to −3.1).
source: The cereal specific declines in grains are as follows: wheat (−7.6%, −9.3 to −5.9), rice (−7.2%, −11.3 to −3.1), and barley (−6.9%, −10.5 to −3.2) (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis for specific cereal crops.

claim: The cereal specific decline in barley grains is −6.9% (−10.5 to −3.2).
source: The cereal specific declines in grains are as follows: wheat (−7.6%, −9.3 to −5.9), rice (−7.2%, −11.3 to −3.1), and barley (−6.9%, −10.5 to −3.2) (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analysis for specific cereal crops.

claim: Wheat and rice alone provide over 40% of calories to humans.
source: This is notable because wheat and rice alone provide over 40% of calories to humans.
evidence: This is a statement about the nutritional importance of wheat and rice, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: The CO2-induced shift in the plant ionome is empirically robust—evident in both artificial (chambers, greenhouses) and field (FACE) conditions.
source: Empirically robust—evident in both artificial (chambers, greenhouses) and field (FACE) conditions (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the meta-analysis comparing different experimental conditions.

claim: The CO2-induced shift in the plant ionome is geographically pervasive—found in temperate and subtropical/tropical regions.
source: Geographically pervasive—found in temperate and subtropical/tropical regions (Figures 7 and 8).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the geographical analysis of the meta-analysis data.

claim: The CO2-induced shift in the plant ionome is systemic—affecting herbaceous and woody plants, crops, and wild plants, photosynthetic and edible tissues, including wheat, rice, and barley grains.
source: Systemic—affecting herbaceous and woody plants, crops, and wild plants, photosynthetic and edible tissues, including wheat, rice, and barley grains (Figures 3, 4 and 8).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the meta-analysis across different plant groups and tissues.

claim: The effect of eCO2 on N is nearly twice as large as its mean effect on minerals.
source: Not only does eCO2 reduce the plant mineral content, but it also alters plant stoichiometry. Specifically, the effect of eCO2 on N is nearly twice as large as its mean effect on minerals.
evidence: This is an inference from the data showing differential effects on N versus minerals.

claim: The differential effect of eCO2 on N (15%), and P (9%) and S (9%) translates into a ∼7% reduction in the plant N:P and N:S.
source: The differential effect of eCO2 on N (15%), and P (9%) and S (9%) translates into a ∼7% reduction in the plant N:P and N:S.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the observed effects on individual elements.

claim: eCO2 increases C:P and C:S by 16%, and C:N by 25%.
source: It follows then that eCO2 increases C:P and C:S by 16%, and C:N by 25% confirming the previous findings of 19–27% higher C:N in plants grown in eCO2 (Poorter et al., 1997; Stiling and Cornelissen, 2007; Robinson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the observed effects, confirmed by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous findings show 19–27% higher C:N in plants grown in eCO2.
source: It follows then that eCO2 increases C:P and C:S by 16%, and C:N by 25% confirming the previous findings of 19–27% higher C:N in plants grown in eCO2 (Poorter et al., 1997; Stiling and Cornelissen, 2007; Robinson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Poorter et al., 1997; Stiling and Cornelissen, 2007; Robinson et al., 2012.

claim: Only two CO2 studies report selenium (Se) content.
source: Only two CO2 studies report selenium (Se) content (Högy et al., 2009, 2013), and none report data on tin (Sn), lithium (Li), and most other trace-elements.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability supported by citations to Högy et al., 2009, 2013.

claim: No CO2 studies report data on tin (Sn), lithium (Li), and most other trace-elements.
source: Only two CO2 studies report selenium (Se) content (Högy et al., 2009, 2013), and none report data on tin (Sn), lithium (Li), and most other trace-elements.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability based on the literature search.

claim: eCO2 boosts TNC concentration by 10–45%.
source: Out of the two types of carbohydrates, eCO2 affects stronger the latter, boosting TNC concentration by 10–45% (Stiling and Cornelissen, 2007; Robinson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stiling and Cornelissen, 2007; Robinson et al., 2012.

claim: eCO2 tends to lower protein in plant tissues.
source: Furthermore, eCO2 tends to lower protein in plant tissues (Taub et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Taub et al., 2008.

claim: eCO2 should exacerbate the inverse relationship found between TNC and protein.
source: Hence, we can reason that eCO2 should exacerbate the inverse relationship found between TNC and protein (Poorter and Villar, 1997).
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of eCO2 on TNC and protein, supported by citation to Poorter and Villar, 1997.

claim: C:N poorly correlates with TNC:protein because protein is more C-rich than carbohydrates (C content in protein is 52–55% cf. 40–45% in carbohydrates).
source: However, C:N poorly correlates with TNC:protein because protein is more C-rich than carbohydrates (C content in protein is 52–55% cf. 40–45% in carbohydrates).
evidence: This is a statement based on the chemical composition of proteins and carbohydrates.

claim: A higher carbohydrate:protein results in a lower C content.
source: Thus, a higher carbohydrate:protein results in a lower C content.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relative C content of carbohydrates and proteins.

claim: eCO2 can elevate TNC:protein up to fivefold higher than it does C:N.
source: Table 1 compares CO2-induced changes in C:N with respective changes in TNC:protein. It shows that eCO2 can elevate TNC:protein up to fivefold higher than it does C:N.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: New evidence challenges 'the notion that a calorie is a calorie from a metabolic perspective' by showing that changes in dietary carbohydrate:protein:fat ratios affect metabolism and weight gain in humans.
source: New evidence, however, challenges "the notion that a calorie is a calorie from a metabolic perspective" by showing that changes in dietary carbohydrate:protein:fat ratios affect metabolism and weight gain in humans (Ebbeling et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ebbeling et al., 2012.

claim: Obesity could be a form of malnutrition, where increased carbohydrate:protein and excessive carbohydrate consumption could be possible culprits.
source: The new evidence supports an emerging view that while obesity is quantified as an imbalance between energy inputs and expenditures (Hall et al., 2011), it could also be a form of malnutrition (Wells, 2013), where increased carbohydrate:protein (Simpson and Raubenheimer, 2005) and excessive carbohydrate consumption (Taubes, 2013) could be possible culprits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2011; Wells, 2013; Simpson and Raubenheimer, 2005; Taubes, 2013.

claim: The FACE study of Porteaus et al. (2009) reports a 7–8% increase in starch concentrations in wheat grains, which translates to ∼4 g of additional starch per 100 g DM.
source: For example, the FACE study of Porteaus et al. (2009) reports a 7–8% increase in starch concentrations in wheat grains, which translates to ∼4 g of additional starch per 100 g DM.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Porteaus et al., 2009.

claim: Teng et al. (2006) reports that eCO2 increased TNC by 76% in leaves of Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: For example, Teng et al. (2006) reports that eCO2 increased TNC by 76% in leaves of Arabidopsis thaliana.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Teng et al., 2006.

claim: CO2 studies show that—irrespective of the baseline TNC content—eCO2 tends to boost TNC by a few grams (1–8 g) per 100 g DM of plant tissue.
source: More generally, CO2 studies show that—irrespective of the baseline TNC content—eCO2 tends to boost TNC by a few grams (1–8 g) per 100 g DM of plant tissue (Poorter et al., 1997; Keutgen and Chen, 2001; Katny et al., 2005; Erbs et al., 2010; Azam et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Poorter et al., 1997; Keutgen and Chen, 2001; Katny et al., 2005; Erbs et al., 2010; Azam et al., 2013.

claim: WHO (2014) conditionally recommends that intake of free sugars not exceed 5% of total energy, which is equivalent to 5–8 teaspoons of sugar for a typical 2000–3000 kcal/day diet.
source: These questions are better left for nutritionists, but it is worth noting that WHO (2014) conditionally recommends that intake of free sugars not exceed 5% of total energy, which is equivalent to 5–8 teaspoons of sugar for a typical 2000–3000 kcal/day diet.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2014.

claim: 'Hidden hunger' is currently the world's most widespread nutritional disorder.
source: 'Hidden hunger'—stems from poorly diversified plant-based diets meeting caloric but not nutritional needs. It is currently the world's most widespread nutritional disorder (Kennedy et al., 2003; Welch and Graham, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kennedy et al., 2003; Welch and Graham, 2005.

claim: 'Hidden hunger' lowers the GDP of the most afflicted countries by 2–5% and is partly responsible for their Third World status.
source: It lowers the GDP of the most afflicted countries by 2–5% and is partly responsible for their Third World status (WHO, 2002; Stein, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to WHO, 2002; Stein, 2009.

claim: A billion people still have no regular access to iodized table salt, making iodine deficiency the leading cause of preventable brain damage, cretinism, and lower IQ in children.
source: The case of iodine is illustrative: although iodized table salt nearly wiped out iodine deficiency in the industrialized world, a billion people still have no regular access to it, making iodine deficiency the leading cause of preventable brain damage, cretinism, and lower IQ in children (Welch and Graham, 1999; WHO, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Welch and Graham, 1999; WHO, 2002.

claim: Every third person in the world is at risk of inadequate Zn intake with its deficiency substantially contributing to stunting, compromised immunity, and child mortality.
source: Every third person in the world is at risk of inadequate Zn intake with its deficiency substantially contributing to stunting, compromised immunity, and child mortality (Brown et al., 2001; UNICEF, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 2001; UNICEF, 2009.

claim: Iron deficiency affects at least 2 billion people and is the leading cause of anemia that increases maternal mortality.
source: Iron deficiency affects at least 2 billion people and is the leading cause of anemia that increases maternal mortality (WHO, 2002; UNICEF, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to WHO, 2002; UNICEF, 2009.

claim: Millions are Ca, Mg, and Se deficient, including some population segments of developed countries.
source: Millions are Ca, Mg, and Se deficient (Stein, 2009; White and Broadley, 2009), including some population segments of developed countries (Rayman, 2007; Khokhar et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stein, 2009; White and Broadley, 2009; Rayman, 2007; Khokhar et al., 2012.

claim: Every third adult in the world is overweight or obese.
source: With every third adult in the world being overweight or obese (Keats and Wiggins, 2014), WHO ranks both mineral undernutrition and obesity among the top 20 global health risks (WHO, 2002; Hill et al., 2003; Stein, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Keats and Wiggins, 2014.

claim: WHO ranks both mineral undernutrition and obesity among the top 20 global health risks.
source: With every third adult in the world being overweight or obese (Keats and Wiggins, 2014), WHO ranks both mineral undernutrition and obesity among the top 20 global health risks (WHO, 2002; Hill et al., 2003; Stein, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to WHO, 2002; Hill et al., 2003; Stein, 2009.

claim: Intriguing links have been found between the lower blood serum concentrations of Ca, Cr, Fe, Mg, Mn, Se, Zn, and increased body mass index (BMI), with most of the findings appearing in the last decade.
source: While the role of mineral deficiency in obesity is still unclear, intriguing links have been found between the lower blood serum concentrations of Ca, Cr, Fe, Mg, Mn, Se, Zn, and increased body mass index (BMI), with most of the findings appearing in the last decade (Singh et al., 1998; Martin et al., 2006; Arnaud et al., 2007; García et al., 2009; Payahoo et al., 2013; Yerlikaya et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Singh et al., 1998; Martin et al., 2006; Arnaud et al., 2007; García et al., 2009; Payahoo et al., 2013; Yerlikaya et al., 2013.

claim: The dynamic mathematical model of human metabolism links weight changes to dietary and behavioral changes.
source: The dynamic mathematical model of human metabolism, which links weight changes to dietary and behavioral changes (Hall et al., 2011), can help to quantify the effect of a prolonged 5% increase in food intake.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hall et al., 2011.

claim: For an average moderately active American female, a prolonged 5% increase in food intake results in a weight gain of 4.8 kg over a 3-year period, provided all other aspects of behavior and diet remain unchanged.
source: When parameterized with anthropometric data for an average moderately active American female (age 38, height 163 cm, weight 76 kg, BMI 28.6, energy intake 2431 kcal/day [10171 kJ]) (Fryar et al., 2012; CIA, 2013), the model outputs a weight gain of 4.8 kg over a 3-year period, provided all other aspects of behavior and diet remain unchanged.
evidence: This is a calculation using the Hall et al. model with specific parameters from cited sources.

claim: For an average moderately active American male, a prolonged 5% increase in food intake results in a weight gain of 5.8 kg over a 3-year period.
source: For a male, the respective weight gain is 5.8 kg.
evidence: This is a calculation using the Hall et al. model.

claim: A 4–5% difference in total daily energy intake, a mere 100 kcal/day, could be responsible for most weight gain in the population.
source: The results are congruent with Hill et al. (2003), who argued that a 4–5% difference in total daily energy intake, a mere 100 kcal/day, could be responsible for most weight gain in the population.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hill et al., 2003.

claim: The rise in CO2 levels over the last 18–30 years has already been implicated in higher C assimilation and plant growth.
source: The rise in CO2 levels over the last 18–30 years has already been implicated in the two effects that can influence the plant ionome: higher C assimilation and plant growth (Donohue et al., 2013), and lower transpiration (Keenan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Donohue et al., 2013.

claim: The rise in CO2 levels over the last 18–30 years has already been implicated in lower transpiration.
source: The rise in CO2 levels over the last 18–30 years has already been implicated in the two effects that can influence the plant ionome: higher C assimilation and plant growth (Donohue et al., 2013), and lower transpiration (Keenan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Keenan et al., 2013.

claim: Over the last 250 years, the atmospheric CO2 concentration has increased by 120 ppm.
source: Considering that over the last 250 years, the atmospheric CO2 concentration has increased by 120 ppm—an increase that is not far from the mean 184 ppm enrichment in the FACE studies—it is plausible that plant quality has changed.
evidence: This is a statement about historical CO2 changes, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Declines in mineral concentrations have been found in wild plants and in crop fruits, vegetables, and grains over 22–250 years.
source: Indeed, declines in mineral concentrations have been found in wild plants and in crop fruits, vegetables, and grains over 22–250 years (Penuelas and Matamala, 1993; Duquesnay et al., 2000; Davis et al., 2004; Ekholm et al., 2007; Fan et al., 2008; Jonard et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Penuelas and Matamala, 1993; Duquesnay et al., 2000; Davis et al., 2004; Ekholm et al., 2007; Fan et al., 2008; Jonard et al., 2009.

claim: The mineral declines in crops can be an unintended consequence of the Green Revolution that produced high-yield cultivars with altered mineral content.
source: While the mineral declines in crops can be an unintended consequence of the Green Revolution that produced high-yield cultivars with altered mineral content (Davis et al., 2004; Fan et al., 2008), the reason for the mineral declines in wild plants cannot be attributed to it.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Davis et al., 2004; Fan et al., 2008.

claim: Hersoug et al. (2012) proposed that rising CO2 promotes weight gains and obesity in the human population directly (via breathing) by reducing the pH of blood and, consequently, increasing appetite and energy intake.
source: Can eCO2 directly affect human health? Hersoug et al. (2012) proposed that rising CO2 promotes weight gains and obesity in the human population directly (via breathing) by reducing the pH of blood and, consequently, increasing appetite and energy intake.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hersoug et al., 2012.

claim: Weight gain has been observed in wild mammals, lab animals, and humans over the last several decades.
source: Weight gain has been observed in wild mammals, lab animals, and humans over the last several decades (Klimentidis et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Klimentidis et al., 2011.

claim: Rohde et al. (2013) analyzed 14 million mean monthly local temperature records to uncover the 1.5°C rise in the global average temperature since 1753.
source: For example, Rohde et al. (2013) analyzed 14 million mean monthly local temperature records to uncover the 1.5°C rise in the global average temperature since 1753—undoubtedly a potent but a very small change relative to the variations of tens of degrees in local temperature.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rohde et al., 2013.

claim: The foliar dataset covers 4733 observations of 25 chemical elements in 110 species and cultivars.
source: The foliar dataset covers 4733 observations of 25 chemical elements in 110 species and cultivars.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The edible tissues dataset covers 3028 observations of 23 elements in 41 species and cultivars.
source: The edible tissues dataset covers 3028 observations of 23 elements in 41 species and cultivars.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The FACE studies cover 2264 observations of 24 elements in 25 species and cultivars.
source: The FACE studies cover 2264 observations of 24 elements in 25 species and cultivars.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The two datasets reflect data on 125 C3 and 5 C4 species/cultivars.
source: The two datasets reflect data on 125 C3 and 5 C4 species/cultivars.
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: In the very low power (<0.20) region, the noise completely hides the CO2-induced shift of the plant ionome.
source: Plotting the effect sizes (with 95% CIs) for the 25 minerals against their respective statistical power reveals a clear pattern (Figure 1). In the very low power (<0.20) region, the noise completely hides the CO2-induced shift of the plant ionome.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 1 showing the relationship between statistical power and effect detection.

claim: As the statistical power increases, the direction and the magnitude of the CO2 effect on minerals become increasingly visible.
source: As the statistical power increases, so does the likelihood that a statistically significant result reflects true effect and, consequently, the direction and the magnitude of the CO2 effect on minerals become increasingly visible in the higher power regions of the plot.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 1 showing the relationship between statistical power and effect detection.

claim: Average ambient and elevated CO2 levels across all the studies are 368 ppm and 689 ppm respectively.
source: Average ambient and elevated CO2 levels across all the studies are 368 ppm and 689 ppm respectively.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the CO2 levels in the studies analyzed.

claim: Germany leads the world in the FACE and OTC data generation with the largest number of mean observations of mineral concentrations (285), followed by the USA (218).
source: Germany leads the world in the FACE and OTC data generation with the largest number of mean observations of mineral concentrations (285), followed by the USA (218) (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the geographical analysis of the dataset.

claim: The wheat experiments of Fernando et al. (2014) employed an unprecedented for FACE studies 48 replicates.
source: Though Australia generated only 30 mean observations, it stands out in the exceptional precision of some of its studies: the wheat experiments of Fernando et al. (2014) employed an unprecedented for FACE studies 48 replicates (for this reason, the study is easily identifiable on Figure 9).
evidence: This is a statement about a specific study's methodology, supported by citation to Fernando et al., 2014.

claim: The symmetrical funnel shape of the plot around the mean effect size indicates the publication bias in the dataset is insignificant.
source: The symmetrical funnel shape of the plot around the mean effect size indicates the publication bias in the dataset is insignificant (Egger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an interpretation of Figure 9 based on established methods for detecting publication bias, supported by citation to Egger et al., 1997.
